note: A UNIFORM STRIDE OVER A NETWORK IS A SAMPLE OF WHATEVER THAT NETWORK IS MOSTLY MADE OF. The Rill Task 3 widened the channel network from river cells only to every land cell with a downhill target: seed 42 at level 6 went 183 to 3606 polylines and 883 to 14606 vertices. Three tests that sample the network by stride went red or misleading, all for the same reason and none of them wrong before. (1) windows/locale water_reading the_discharge_clause_makes_the_strongest_crossing_impassable asserts the strongest water in the world is not wadeable; a 400-stride of 14606 vertices now has a max drainage of 48 against a threshold of 80, because the added reaches are all headwaters. A claim that NAMES an extreme must have that extreme in its population - adding the top 25 by discharge is not cherry-picking. (2) the_width_clause_binds_when_the_step_shrinks fell to 37 flips against a floor of 50: the qualifying RATE fell 24 percent to 9 percent because a creek is narrower than both step lengths and is filtered out. Sample more, do not lower the floor - it now reads 146 of 146. (3) windows/lab the_analytic_channel_area_matches_the_sampled_one cost 158.9 s (400 probes per vertex, each linear in the network) and failed at ratio 1.203 against a 0.9 to 1.1 window; strided to 200 vertices it costs 8.6 s and the ratio is 1.1935, so the stride costs no signal. Second lesson from that one: with 6400 confluences instead of 90, a transect at a tributary mouth walks through water the TRUNK owns, so the unrestricted sampled width overstates (1.19x) and the same-line-only width understates (0.83x). They bracket rather than bound. Before you grow a sampled structure, grep for who strides it.
